Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.
Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.

An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.
“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.
It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.
Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.

By Alia ChughtaiPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.
Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.
“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”
The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.
It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.

Arafa Abdelaziz endured a dangerous 15-day journey from Omdurman to a displacement camp in Port Sudan in late 2023, after losing her husband and one of her two sons, who died early in the war.
Her husband died just days after fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, leaving her to care for her remaining two children as their home city of Omdurman in Khartoum State came under bombardment.
Five months later, her eight-year-old son was killed by a stray bullet during clashes near Omdurman’s market.
“My son was playing outside the house with his friends when I suddenly heard a loud noise. When I went outside, I found that his head had been shattered by gunfire,” said the 33-year-old.

item.title: Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown
item.description:
By Nick DeardenPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
SaveShare Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown on social mediashare-nodes
Sharefacebook

Police officers stand next to a fire in a street during clashes on the sideline of a demonstration in Marseille, France on November 21, 2026 [Sylvain Thomas/AFP]
Europe is in the grips of a “hot autumn”. For several weeks now, French students have led mass protests against underinvestment in education, teacher shortages and dilapidated classrooms.
In Spain, mass protests broke out after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years, after her rent was hiked by 230 percent by an investment fund that bought the property. She died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Now the protests are spreading: to Italy, where upwards of one million people took to the streets of 50 cities last week; to Portugal, where tent encampments have sprung up to oppose rapid hikes in housing costs; to Germany, where riot police with water cannon confronted protesters opposing the creeping extension of conscription; and most recently, to the United Kingdom, where thousands of students joined a day of action on November 20 under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars!”
The common thread which has sparked these Gen Z protests is the rapidly rising cost of living. In the wake of the global pandemic, the war in Ukraine, US tariffs, and now the US-Israel war on Iran, global supply chains are breaking down, sending costs spiralling.
But this is only a symptom of a wider problem. Deregulation and neoliberal policies have allowed corporations to take over not only the economy but also politics. This has led to massive wealth concentration at the top and increasing precarity for the vast majority of the European population.
